rows.verified: Employers must protect workers against risks from lead under the Control of Lead at Work Regulations 2002.
Lead assessments should identify tasks that use lead or generate lead dust or fume.
HSE presents lead control through an Assess, Control and Review approach.
Lead exposure can cause serious health effects including anaemia and kidney disease.
Control guidance covers handling, processing, repair, maintenance, storage and disposal activities involving lead.
Relevant exposure forms include inhalable dust, vapour or fumes and ingestible powder, dust, paint or paste.
Employers must prevent lead exposure or, where prevention is not reasonably practicable, control it.
HSE advises good exposure-control practice because health effects may occur below statutory suspension levels.
Lead risk depends on lead form, concentration, task, exposure route, duration, controls, hygiene and worker susceptibility.
HSE lead evidence is substance-, task-, workplace-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease probability.
Metalworking fluids can cause dermatitis and occupational lung disease.
COSHH requires exposure by inhalation, ingestion or skin contact to be prevented or adequately controlled.
Fluid quality and bacterial contamination should be monitored and managed.
Skin exposure should be minimised during machining and sump cleaning.
Airborne mist should be prevented or controlled, including by enclosure and local exhaust ventilation.
Health surveillance is required where exposure to fluid or mist cannot be prevented.
Water-mix wash fluids can present skin and respiratory hazards similar to machining fluids.
Using compressed air to dry contaminated components can generate mist that requires containment or extraction.
Metalworking-fluid risk depends on formulation, machining process, mist generation, microbial contamination, controls, skin contact and worker susceptibility.
HSE metalworking-fluid evidence is fluid-, machine-, task-, workplace-, worker- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
